newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Freed Palestinian has no regrets over dead soldier.
newsitem.headline: Freed Palestinian has no regrets over dead soldier.

text.p: A Brazilian woman of Palestinian descent who was released from an Israeli prison this week said on Thursday she had no regrets about her role in the 1984 killing of a 20-year-old Israeli Army sergeant.
"It was not personal ... it was an act of war," Lamia Maarouf told reporters at her home shortly after returning to Brazil.
"Regret? That word does not belong in my vocabulary," she said. "We were warriors just like the Israelis, except we had no uniforms, no planes, no tanks."
Maarouf, 32, was deported to Brazil on Wednesday after serving 11 years of a life sentence for her role in the killing of Sgt. David Manous.

Manous was hitchhiking when he was picked up by Maarouf and her husband, Taufic Ibrahim, both of whom were involved in the Al Fatah Palestinian liberation movement. Manous was shot by Ibrahim, who is still serving time in prison.
Maarouf, freed on Wednesday, was one of 30 Palestinian women whose release was agreed in 1995 between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Far from apologising for her involvement in guerrilla activities, Maarouf said it was the determination of people like herself that allowed the peace process to start.
"Just the other day (Palestinian President) Yasser Arafat said he wouldn't be where he is today if it weren't for the prisoners," Maarouf said.
Maarouf's story has brought home the violence of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to many Brazilians, who normally consider the problems in the Middle East as a foreign and distant tragedy.
Hundreds of family members, sympathisers and journalists packed into Sao Paulo's Cumbica's airport on Thursday to welcome Maarouf back to Brazil.
But leaders of the Jewish community said they were concerned the Brazilian press coverage would transform Maarouf into a heroine.

"As a rabbi I support her liberation within the context of the peace process. However, I hope she is received as what she is, and not as a heroine." said Rabbi Henry Sobel of the Sao Paulo Jewish Congregation.
Sobel said he had refused an invitation to meet Maarouf at the airport.
Maarouf, who has an 11-year-old daughter, said she was working to obtain permission to return to Israel so that she could remain close to her jailed husband.
"I am a freedom fighter. But now we must fight for peace," she said.
